title.en: Coyote and his Son: The Eagle-Tree to the Sky Country

region.en: Eagle-tree mountain near Snake River, up to the sky country (symbolic pin at Waha Lake)
region.zh: 斯內克河畔神樹之山，直上天界（象徵定位於瓦哈湖）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; edited by Theresa Mayer; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 1. Coyote and his Son' (collected by Farrand)

summary.en: Old-Coyote, coveting his son's white Duck wife, sends him to strip and climb for eaglets in a tree that rises with every wink of the father's eye until it carries the youth beyond the clouds into the sky country. There he finds a five-doored tent of his grandfathers, who spend five days making rope enough to lower him in a huge spoon through five cloud-obstacles — 'Roll over when you feel the spoon stop' — down to the earth. In the meantime Old-Coyote has donned the son's clothes and deceived the Duck wife, while the sceptical Beetle wife leaves with her baby; the returned son overtakes them, Raven proves Old-Coyote a liar, the people shout the true news, and Duck, ashamed, becomes a duck in the river forever.
summary.zh: 老郊狼覬覦其子之白鴨妻，誘其脫衣攀樹取鷹雛；父每眨眼一次，樹便升高一截，終將其子送上雲霄天界。其子在天界遇五位祖父之五門大帳，祖父等費五日搓繩，以巨勺盛之，穿五重雲障縋其下凡——『勺停即翻身』。其間老郊狼穿上其子衣物，騙得鴨妻；多疑之甲蟲妻携子離去。其子歸來追上妻兒，渡鴉揭穿老郊狼謊言，眾人齊呼真相；鴨妻羞愧，化為鴨，永居河中。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin (Yakama-area) narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Two further versions are recorded in the source. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote had a son who was a chief and a good man. He went up a mountain near Snake River; one morning he kicked a log, and fire came, which would burn to warm people, and he used to tell the people to hunt deer — all considered him the greatest chief. Coyote's son had two wives, Beetle, who was black, and Duck, who was white, and Beetle had a son. One day Old-Coyote made a fire of willows, saw the women's privates between their legs as the sparks flew, and coveted Duck. He resolved to kill his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 135 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He told the women that there was an eagle with several young ones on the top of a tree, and they immediately said they wanted the feathers; Old-Coyote told his son to get the eaglets at once, since they would fly away in about ten days. They came to a mountain covered with trees, and Coyote showed his son the eyry on a tree that did not seem very high and was easy to climb; he said he could not climb it himself, and sent his son, telling him to strip off his clothes so they should not be spoiled — Old-Coyote wanted the clothes for himself. The youth had gone a little way when the old man winked his eye at him, and the eyry rose; he winked again, and it rose still higher. The youth turned and scolded his father, who said he was just watching him. The youth kept on climbing until he was out of sight: the tree carried him up beyond the clouds, into the sky country, and when he left the tree it had shrunk back to its original size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 135 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sky country was just like our earth. After a while he saw a large tent with five doors; at the first the people shouted that it was cold, at the next they seized their spears to attack him, and at the last they tried to hit him with their spears — until he shouted, 'Stop, grandfather!' They answered, 'Our only grandchild is Coyote's son.' — 'I am he,' he said, and they welcomed him, gave him food, and promised to send him down. They had long ropes piled up in coils, and told him it would take five days to make enough to reach down to the earth, asking him to fill the spoon with deer-tallow to rub on their hands, which would be sore from letting him down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 135-136 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the end of five days they put him into a spoon as large as a huge dish, instructing him to roll over in it whenever he felt it stop. He went down through the sky, struck obstacles five times — the clouds through which he was passing — and rolled over each time; finally he struck solid ground, and when the spoon did not move he knew he had reached the earth. He untied himself, hunted deer as requested, filled the spoon with tallow, and pulled the rope as a signal that he had arrived. In the meantime Old-Coyote had gone home and taken the Duck wife, deceiving her by pretending to be her husband; he danced all the time, telling the people he had persuaded his father to climb up, and most of the people believed him, because he looked so different. Duck actually thought he was her husband, but Beetle disbelieved him, put reeds on her back, placed her baby on them, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 136 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote's son followed her, passing ten of her camp-sites, taking along the boy's bow found at the last. Looking down over a hill, he saw his wife carrying the child and crying; the boy saw his father and cried, 'Father has my bow!' — 'Your father is dead,' said the mother. Catching up to them, he held her by stepping on her rawhide strap, and said, 'Don't strike the boy! You are hurting him.' Then they sat down, and he related all that had happened; she told him how the people had missed him, because without him they did not kill many deer. He told his wife to wrap him up in reeds, place the boy on top of him, and stop at some distance from the camp; she was to keep crying, because her child was hungry, and inform him if the people caught a fat deer. Mosquito volunteered to look through a hole in the tent-cover and was driven back; Raven slipped in silently under the tent, saw Coyote's son eating, recognized him, and told what he had seen, proving that Old-Coyote was a liar. The old people gave orders to everybody to shout, 'Coyote's son has come back!' Old-Coyote pulled off his clothes, jumped into the fire, and cried over his boy; Duck was ashamed and turned into a duck, and has been in the river ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 136-137 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Hill named Backbone (Kupkup) close to the river, near Waka Lake (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河畔之脊骨嶺（Kupkup），瓦哈湖附近（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 1. Coyote and his Son' (revenge on Old-Coyote)

summary.en: From that time on Old-Coyote was treated like a slave, and Coyote's son decided to take revenge. Hunting on a ridge near Waka Lake, close to the river by the hill named Backbone (Kupkup), he killed a fat deer, butchered it and left it there, then sent Old-Coyote to bring in the carcass with a strap Beetle had painted to look like a tump-line. The strap broke five times; hot and exhausted, Old-Coyote could go no farther, and Coyote's son threw the backbone down the hill, saying, 'Henceforth this shall be Backbone Ridge' — and Old-Coyote sat down ashamed.
summary.zh: 自那時起，老郊狼形同奴僕。郊狼之子謀復仇，於瓦哈湖附近脊骨嶺（Kupkup）下河邊獵得肥鹿，剖而留之，遣老郊狼以甲蟲妻繪成背帶之假革帶負屍而歸。革帶五斷；天熱力竭，老郊狼寸步難行。郊狼之子遂擲鹿脊下山，曰：『自此此嶺名脊骨嶺。』老郊狼愧而坐地。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: From that time on, Old-Coyote was treated like a slave. Coyote's son decided to take revenge. He went hunting on a ridge near Waka Lake, and came to a hill named Backbone (Kupkup); there, close to the river, he killed a fat deer, butchered it, and left it there. Then he went home and asked Old-Coyote to bring in the carcass. Beetle had painted a gut like a tump-line; they gave it to Old-Coyote to carry the carcass. When Old-Coyote reached the deer, he took a great piece off and ate it; then he tied up the pack and started to carry it home. He had gone but a little way when the strap broke. His son told him to tie it together and go ahead. The strap broke five times, and finally he had nothing with which to carry his burden; he grew very tired. It was hot, and he could not go any farther. Then Coyote's son threw the backbone down the hill, saying, 'Henceforth this shall be Backbone Ridge.' Then Old-Coyote sat down ashamed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 137 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Swallow dams on the Columbia and Snake rivers (symbolic pin at the Dalles)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河與斯內克河燕子姊妹之壩（象徵定位於達爾斯）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 2. Coyote liberates the Salmon' (collected by Farrand)

summary.en: Five Swallow girls own a dam and fish-trap that hold all the salmon back from the upper river. Coyote turns himself into a crying infant drifting on a reed-and-buffalo-skin raft; the girls, who have always wanted a child, race for him, and the eldest wins. The baby grows with unnatural speed, calls every part of her body 'my mother's', cries his way to a full meal and all their water, and when sent for more runs like a man between terraces. At the hut he eats the stores, tears down the dam — 'There shall no longer be a dam in this river. Many Indians will come here to live' — shouts the news, ties a head-sized spoon on as a helmet against their blows, and vanishes into a cloud of black paint. The salmon crowd up the river behind him; when his old reed blanket tears at every catch, Beaver advises the club, and the killed salmon is cooked while Coyote sleeps.
summary.zh: 五燕子姊妹壩上蓄魚，阻鮭上溯。郊狼化為啼哭嬰兒，臥蘆葦野皮筏順流而下；眾姊妹久盼子嗣，競游搶之，長姊得勝。嬰孩速長，凡觸母身皆喚『吾母之……』；索食索水，撒潑放賴，得令自取則人立而行，過兩層臺地仍佯為嬰孩爬行。至屋飽食存糧，拆壩放水——『此河從此無壩，印第安人將大量遷來』——以勺為盔禦棒擊，撒黑漆遁入黑暗。鮭魚成群上溯；其舊葦毯屢捕屢裂，河貍教以棍擊，烹鮭而眠。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Three versions are recorded in the source; the salmon-liberation element is common to all. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote knew of five girls who prevented the salmon from coming up the river. He went in that direction, and sat down to think out how he might obtain the salmon. 'I will turn into an infant and float down on a bed of reeds,' he said to himself. 'The women will take care of me and raise me until I know their customs.' When the girls saw the infant drifting on the water, they rescued it; the oldest girl said, 'He shall be my son.' She kept him; and when he grew up and came to be a young man, he saw that the salmon were kept in a pound. He cut a ditch and made a channel, which enabled the salmon to go up the river; he showed his mother how he had broken the dam. The women tried to kill him, but he escaped and came back home; then he went down and freed all the people who were held captive in the form of fishes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 139 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the second version, he swam all the way down the Snake River without once turning around, and came to the dam of five Swallow girls who owned it and a fish-trap. He turned into a little boy drifting down on a raft of reeds and buffalo-skin, crying lustily; the girls had always wanted a child, and raced to see who should get this one — Coyote winked his eye at the oldest, who drew ahead and won. They had had him but two days when he began to eat; in three days he began to creep about and to talk. Sleeping beside his mother, he felt of her head, her hair, her body, repeating 'my mother's' of every part; the youngest of the girls knew the baby was Coyote, and every time she said so he began to cry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 140-141 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Five days elapsed in this manner; on the sixth they planned to dig roots and took the baby along with water and food. He ate everything and drank all the water, then cried for more, until they told him to go and get it himself. He crawled down the hill, got up and ran when out of sight at the first terrace, crawled again in sight, and ran once more after the second; soon he arrived at the house, ate all the food in it, and tore down the dam in the river, digging around it. When the water began to come through he sat down and called out, 'Come down, the dam is broken!' The youngest said, 'I know that is Coyote's work.' The fish were running up in shoals; Coyote had made a spoon just the size of his head and tied it on, so that when his mother hit him on the head he did not feel it and just laughed. He untied a bag of black paint, and immediately it became dark so they could not see him; from a hill he called down to them to take care of his children if he should have any — 'The youngest one knew me, so perhaps she will not have a baby' — nevertheless he gave them all names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 141 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the third version the Swallow girls lived at the Dalles on the Columbia River, where they had made a dam to prevent the salmon from going upstream. The baby grew up very quickly, and the youngest girl suspected there was something strange about him and concluded it was Coyote and no real baby at all. When he had finished eating the stores, he began to tear down the dam, saying, 'There shall no longer be a dam in this river. Many Indians will come here to live'; when he had broken it, he shouted, 'Mother, come down! Our dam is broken, and the water is gone.' The youngest scolded the others and told them the baby was none other than Coyote. The salmon now crowded up the river, and Coyote followed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 142-143 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Riverbank cook-fire of the Columbia-Salmon country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞鮭鄉河畔炊火處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 2. Coyote liberates the Salmon' (the Wolves and the eggs)

summary.en: Five Wolves smell the cooked salmon and, careful not to awaken Coyote, eat it all, then slit his anus from behind, take out the gut and roast it for him; waking, Coyote thanks his 'grand-daughter' for the food and eats it until a bird shouts, 'You are eating your own guts!' Feeling up to his elbow in the cavity, he puts the last piece back, then hits his hip so that dung becomes boys, all but the youngest returning into him — the youngest tells him the thieves were the Wolves and a Fox. Coyote follows them, eats their ground-oven eggs but leaves one for each, remodels their faces asleep — pulling out noses, pushing in cheeks, making them gray as wolves are now — rubs Fox with egg-yolk for his color, makes Skunk black and white, and laughs at them from the hill; Fox, the swiftest, catches up and sits down with him to talk, for he is Coyote's best friend.
summary.zh: 五狼嗅得熟鮭，躡足盡食，又自後割開郊狼後竅，取出其腸烤以奉之。郊狼醒，謝『孫女』贈食，食之津津；飛鳥高呼：『爾正食己腸！』探手入腔至肘，方納最後一段歸位。再擊其臀，糞化童子，皆歸其身，唯幼者留外告之：竊賊乃五狼一狐。郊狼追至狼巢，食其地灶之蛋，每獸留一枚；趁其酣睡重塑其面——拉長其鼻、按平其頰、染其灰色——以蛋黃塗狐定其色，以黑白定臭鼬之色，立於山頭大笑。狐最捷，追及，然與郊狼並坐而談——蓋狐乃其至交。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Five Wolves smelled the fish and came close to the fire; they found the salmon and ate it, careful not to awaken Coyote. When they had eaten it all, they cut open Coyote's anus, took out the gut, and cooked it for him. When Coyote awoke, he thought, 'There is my fish cooking for me' — but nothing was left but the bones. When he saw the guts, he said, 'My grandchild must have left these guts here,' and began to eat them. A bird saw him, and shouted, 'You are eating your own guts!' Nevertheless he kept on eating, until he felt behind him and ran his hand clear up to his elbow, finding but a little piece of his intestines left, which he put back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 141-142 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he hit his hip a second time, and the dung which appeared turned into boys as before; all but the youngest went back into him. He told Coyote that the thieves were the Wolves and a Fox, who were cooking some eggs and had taken his salmon while he had been asleep. Coyote was very angry, and started out to hunt the Wolves. He came to the place where they were cooking eggs; not far away the Wolves were asleep. The eggs were done, and Coyote began to eat them — he did not eat all, however, but left six, one for each of the animals, and covered them up as they had been before. The Wolves and the Fox slept on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 142 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote took some charcoal and painted their faces to make them look ugly; he painted Fox with the yolk of an egg, and put charcoal on the tips of his ears. When he had finished, Coyote went to a notch on the hill and waited to see what would happen, carrying five bags of black paint. Soon one of the Wolves awoke and called the others; they went to get the eggs, and each took one. Coyote, way up on the hill, laughed to himself; when they went to get another egg, they found nothing but shells, and wondered what the trouble was. One looked at another: 'Why, what is the matter with you?' Then they teased one another about their looks — Fox was yellow all over. They came to the conclusion that this was Coyote's handiwork, and indeed there was Coyote laughing at them. They gave chase, and Fox almost caught him; but Coyote said, 'We are friends,' opened a sack of paint and disappeared in the darkness. When it cleared up, he was on the other side of the canyon, still laughing; so they decided to leave him alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 142 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Goose brothers' camp across the river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雁兄營地，河之彼岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (the marriage)

summary.en: After the strange object that struck his face and cooked like fat meat cost Coyote all his teeth, he finds the camp of five white geese who have flown across the river to hunt deer, leaving their pretty sister alone making clothes, with the promise that any man who chances to their camp shall be her husband. Peering through the tent-hole, Coyote magically provides five eagle feathers tipped with black, five fine men's dresses and five bows and arrows, has made himself a handsome man with nice long hair — but cannot bite the meat she sets before him and must be satisfied with pounded meat. Asleep with open mouth, he is given a set of mountain-sheep teeth by the girl: 'My teeth always do that, they grow while I sleep.' When the five brothers come home and crowd him toward their sister, the eldest says, 'Don't be mean!' — and Coyote married the girl.
summary.zh: 郊狼誤食擊面之異物，牙齒盡落。行至五白雁之營——雁兄五人已渡河獵鹿，留美貌之妹獨自縫衣，且曾言：『凡至此營之男子，不論老幼，皆為其夫。』郊狼窺帳見之，以法術備禮：黑尖鷹羽五支、男服五套、弓箭五副，又自化俊男、蓄美髯。惜無齒難噬，只得就肉糜。睡中張口，雁女見其無齒，乃取大角羊齒一套納其口中：『吾齒向來如此，睡中自長。』五兄歸，屢令其挪位擠向其妹，長兄斥曰：『休得無禮！』郊狼遂娶雁女。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The opening episode in which Coyote cooks and eats a mysterious object and loses his teeth is summarized plainly, as recorded. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote went on up the river. He heard a noise, and saw what he believed to be a duck flying above him. It came nearer, and, as he turned around to look at it, it slapped him in the eye and stuck there. Only with the most strenuous efforts could he dislodge it; when he finally succeeded in removing it, he looked at it, but even then he did not know what it was. He threw it into the river and went on his way; this happened four times. When it struck him the fifth time, he decided to cook it: he pulled it off, cut it up, made a fire of pine-cones, and broiled it on a stick. It smelled just like fat meat; when it was done, he tasted it, and found it tasted like cow-teats. He ate it all up, and when he had finished, he regretted that he had eaten it. He was thirsty, and looked for water; soon he found a good spring, and stooped over to drink. As he opened his mouth, all his teeth fell out; not a single one was left. So he went his way without any teeth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 144-145 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He came to a place where five white geese had their camp. They had flown over the river to hunt deer, and had left their pretty sister at home alone making clothes; before leaving her they had told her that any man who chanced to come to their camp would be her husband, no matter whether he was old or young. Coyote came along, and when he saw the big tent he peeked in through a hole: the girl was sitting making fine things, and he saw how handsome she was. He went back some distance, and by magic procured five eagle's feathers tipped with black, five fine dresses for men, and five bows and arrows, leaving these outside; he had previously made himself a handsome man with nice long hair. The girl received him, cooked food for him, and gave him a fork made of bone; Coyote took a big piece, for he had forgotten all about the loss of his teeth, and could not bite it — he had to be satisfied with pounded meat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 145 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he had finished eating, he lay on his back and sang a song, and soon fell asleep. As he lay there, his mouth was open, and the girl saw that he had no teeth; she took a set of teeth of a mountain-sheep and put them into his mouth, then awakened him. She gave him more food, and he found he could eat with ease. 'My teeth always do that,' he said to the girl; 'they grow while I sleep.' He soon finished all she had placed before him, and told her, 'Here are some clothes that I brought for your brothers.' She thought well of his liberality, and told him her five brothers would be home in the evening. Soon they heard them approach: the eldest came in and threw down his deer, and Coyote thought what a handsome man he was. He told Coyote to move over, and Coyote moved closer to the girl; so with each one of them, until finally the fifth came in and told him to move still closer — by this time he was almost on the girl's lap. The eldest said, 'Don't be mean!' Then Coyote married the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 145-146 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Goose Flight and the Sister's Revenge

region.en: Flight across the river of the goose brothers (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雁兄弟渡河飛翔之處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (the flight and death of Coyote)

summary.en: Allowed at last to hunt with the brothers, Coyote clings to two of them as they fly across the river uttering the goose-cry — until he screams and all fall. He shoots a fawn, swims with the guts tangled around him in shame, and on the crossing home he shouts in midstream despite their rebukes; the youngest says, 'Let us drop him! It is Coyote,' and he falls — 'Be feathers' lets him float down gently, 'Be a limb' drops him again, until, close to the water, he mistakes and says 'Be a limb,' strikes the bottom of the river, and kills himself. At home the girl sews until she breaks her needle — five needles before she lays down her work — puts her heart into her little finger, and shoots her brothers, killing three; only the two youngest are spared, and the elder of these shoots the end of her little finger, killing his sister.
summary.zh: 郊狼終得隨雁兄狩獵：眾雁脱衣化雁，銜其飛渡大河，囑其勿聲。行至中流，郊狼大呼，眾皆墮地。獲幼鹿後，他携腸下水，腸纏其身，羞愧難當；歸途再渡，中流又呼，弟曰：『丟下他吧！是郊狼！』眾乃棄之。郊狼下墜，呼『化為羽毛』而緩降，呼『化為枯枝』而復墜；臨水誤呼『枯枝』，觸河底而亡。家中雁女縫衣屢折針——折五針方罷——知其夫已死；藏心於小指，取弓射兄，誅其三；二弟倖免，弟射其小指尖，妹亦斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The brothers considered Coyote a fine man, and were greatly pleased with the presents he had given to them. Coyote stayed at home one day; the following day he wanted to accompany the brothers when they went hunting. His wife told him that the brothers were accustomed to hunt on the other side of the river, and did not want him to go along because they were going so far that he could not follow them; but the youngest brother said, 'Oh, let him come along!' They came to the river, where they took off their clothes and started to fly across, telling Coyote to utter no sound. Then they flew up into the air, while he clung to two of them; they uttered the goose-cry, and thus they crossed the river. It did not take long before Coyote began to scream, and as soon as he did so, they all fell down. They rebuked him and told him to keep quiet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 146 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: They went on for a short distance, hunting for mountain-sheep and other big game. Soon a fawn appeared, and Coyote shot it; he skinned it and went down to the river, thinking that he had done enough. He took the guts and all with him, and after having walked down along the bank a little way, went in swimming. The Goose brothers came up to him to see what he had caught; they took the fawn and threw it into the river, and the guts caught Coyote around the body. He was ashamed. Then the oldest brother suggested that they cross back; they made ready their packs and prepared to cross, putting Coyote on top of them. They flew up and uttered their cry; in the middle of the stream Coyote began to shout, and they fell down fast. They told him to keep still, but he refused to do so. The youngest brother then said, 'Let us drop him! It is Coyote.' They did so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 146 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he was just above the surface of the water, he said to himself, 'Be feathers,' and he floated through the air gently; when he rose to a great height, he said, 'Be a limb,' and he fell again rapidly. He kept this up until he finally made a mistake, saying, when he was close to the water, 'Be a limb.' He fell, struck the bottom of the river, and killed himself. The girl at home kept on sewing until she broke her needle; then she knew that her brothers had killed her husband. She broke five needles before she laid down her work; then she took the bows and arrows, put her heart into her little finger, and made ready to kill her brothers. When they came near, she began to shoot; they shouted, 'Don't be angry, your husband was Coyote!' She, however, killed three of her brothers, and spared only the two youngest ones. The younger one then said to the elder, 'Shoot the end of her little finger.' He did so, and so killed his sister. Then they decided to leave the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 146-147 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Daughters of Winter and Summer

region.en: House of Winter and house of Summer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冬之屋與夏之屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (Winter and Summer)

summary.en: Fifteen days without food after killing their sister, the two surviving goose brothers eat their bowstring and bow-backing, then reach the house of an old gray-haired giant full of ice without a fire, stark naked, whose little daughter Winter calls her four elder sisters from their underground house to cook for him; hearing how the visitors were treated, the brothers leave. Soon they come to the tent of Summer, very warm, where a fine-dressed little girl brings five dishes of meat — one tiny, four large; the brothers can hardly finish the tiny dish, and the girl's elder sisters comb their tangled hair, so the brothers had two wives. They built a sweat-house, repaired their bows, hunted ten deer a day, and had plenty of meat.
summary.zh: 誅妹之後，二雁弟絕糧十五日，食弓弦與弓背筋而活。終至一灰髮老怪之家：滿屋是冰，無火，老怪裸體，幼女冬兒奉命召四姊出地窖為其炊食。二弟見狀即離去。旋至夏神之帳，暖如春暉；小女衣著華美，奉上五盤肉——一小四大。二弟連小盤亦難食盡。老怪命諸女為客梳其糾結之髮，二弟遂得二妻。二人搭汗屋，修弓矢，日獵十鹿，衣食豐足。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-house episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: They went on, taking along only their bows and arrows. They took no food with them, and had nothing to eat for fifteen days; the younger brother almost starved. His brother took his bowstring and the backing of the bow, both of which were made of sinew, and gave them to him to eat. Finally they came in sight of a large house. They went in. An old gray-haired giant was living there who had four grown daughters and a little one; the youngest girl's name was Winter (xa'lpxa'lp). The house was full of ice and without even a little fire; the old man was stark naked. The four older girls had an underground house to themselves, and were working on beautiful clothing outside the house. The giant sent Winter to call her sisters: as she threw the door open, they shouted, 'You dirty thing! why do you come here?' She delivered her message, and the sisters promised to come soon, cooking a large dishful of food for their father; while they were leaving, the little girl brought two spoons and ate the food with her father, and between them they ate it all. When the young men saw all this, they left.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 147 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon they came to another tent, which belonged to Summer. They entered, and saw an old man and a small girl in a fine dress; the house was very warm. The old man sent the girl to ask her sisters to cook a meal, and they came and prepared five dishes of meat — a very tiny one and four large ones. The brothers asked the old man and the little girl for some food, and were given spoons; the younger one began to eat, and could not finish what was given to him; the elder one then ate, and was hardly able to finish what his brother had left. Thereupon the old man told the girl to put away the rest of the food for them. The hair of the brothers was very much entangled; therefore the old man sent the girl to call her sisters, who were to comb the hair of the brothers — the oldest two girls combed the hair of the elder brother, while the younger girls combed the hair of the younger one, so they had two wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 147-148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers made their home there. They built a sweat-house and repaired their bows, the strings and backing of which they had eaten. The old man told them that there were many deer in the canyons; they set out before daylight and killed ten, which they carried home. They went out to hunt every day, and had plenty of meat, part of which they dried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
